teile.einleitung: A session is the period in which the Swiss parliament sits. Each year there are four ordinary sessions of three weeks each. Sometimes parliament also holds extraordinary sittings or even meets outside Bern.
wichtigste: The spring session takes place in March, the summer session in June.
The winter session lasts from the end of November into December.
The National Council and the Council of States sit at the same time, but in separate chambers.
A quarter of the members of a chamber or the Federal Council can call for an extraordinary session.
A session outside Bern is called “extra muros”.
In May 2020 parliament met in the halls of Bernexpo because of COVID.

abschnitte.text: The parliamentary year begins with the **spring session** in **March**. In **June** comes the **summer session**, and in autumn the autumn session. The **winter session** begins at the end of November and lasts into December. After that there is a longer break until March. Each ordinary session lasts three weeks.

The **National Council** and the **Council of States** sit on the same days, but in separate chambers in the Federal Palace. That way business can pass quickly from one chamber to the other. Both chambers must approve a law for it to apply.

Sometimes urgent business has to be dealt with quickly. Then an **extraordinary session** can take place. It can be called for by a **quarter** of the members of a chamber or by the **Federal Council**. The session must concern particular items of business. When it takes place is decided by the **bureaus** of the two chambers. The bureaus also plan the chambers' work in general.

“**Extra muros**” is Latin and means “outside the walls”. This is the name for sessions that do not take place in the Federal Palace in Bern. The spring session of 2001, for example, took place in **Lugano**. Because the Parliament Building was being renovated, parliament met in **Flims** in the canton of the Grisons in autumn 2006. In May 2020 it was not possible to keep distances in the Federal Palace because of the **COVID pandemic**. That is why the extraordinary session took place in the halls of **Bernexpo**.

gewusst: During the COVID pandemic, the Swiss parliament met in exhibition halls.
Parliament has already travelled to Ticino and the Grisons to hold a session there.

teile.einleitung: Swiss Post brings letters and parcels to every home in Switzerland. Its colour is yellow and its symbol is the post horn. With the PostBus it even travels up to mountain villages.
wichtigste: Swiss Post's signature colour is yellow.
The post horn is the symbol of Swiss Post.
The yellow PostBuses also travel to remote mountain villages.
The PostBus horn plays the three notes “Tü-ta-to”.
Swiss postcodes have four digits.
A letter sent by A-Post arrives faster than one sent by B-Post.

abschnitte.text: Postboxes, delivery vans and PostBuses are **yellow**. That way you recognise Swiss Post straight away. Its symbol is the **post horn**. In the past, the coachmen of the mail coach blew the horn when the coach arrived. That way everyone knew the post was there. Swiss Post belongs to the Confederation and has its headquarters in Bern.

The yellow **PostBuses** are buses. They travel over many mountain passes and to remote villages where no train goes. The PostBus has a **three-note horn**. It sounds “Tü-ta-to” and can be heard clearly on winding mountain roads. For many people in the countryside, the PostBus is the most important link to the nearest town.

Every place has a **postcode** with **four digits**. It helps to sort letters quickly. The first digit shows the region. Bern, for example, has the postcode 3000. In the Zurich area, postcodes begin with an 8, for example 8001.

If you send a letter, you can choose. With **A-Post** the letter usually arrives on the next working day. **B-Post** takes longer but is cheaper. Letters and parcels are brought to the houses by **postwomen and postmen**. They often ride a small yellow electric vehicle.

gewusst: The PostBus “Tü-ta-to” is a set of three notes that you can hear from far away on winding mountain roads.
From the postcode you can tell which region a letter comes from.

teile.einleitung: Smartvote is an online voting aid from Switzerland. You answer questions on political topics, and the website shows which candidates and parties think in a similar way. But each person makes their own decision about whom to vote for.
wichtigste: Smartvote is an online voting aid.
It was used for the first time at the parliamentary elections in 2003.
It is run by the independent association Politools in Bern.
The candidates answer the same questionnaire as the voters.
The Smartspider shows political profiles on eight axes.
A recommendation from Smartvote is only a help, not an obligation.

abschnitte.text: On Smartvote you fill in a **questionnaire**. Depending on the version it has 30 to 75 questions; usually there is a short and a detailed version. Beforehand, the **candidates** answer the same questions themselves. Smartvote then compares the answers. At the end you see a list of the candidates and parties that best match your own answers.

A first public version was created in **2003** for the federal elections. Since 2004 the association **Politools** has run the voting aid. It is politically and religiously **independent** and has its headquarters in **Bern**. Since then Smartvote has been used in many elections at federal, cantonal and municipal level.

The **Smartspider** is a chart that looks like a spider's web. It has **eight axes**, one for each topic area, for example environmental protection or an open foreign policy. The further out a point lies, the more strongly you agree with that goal. This makes profiles easy to compare. The **FDP**, for example, is typically far out on the axis **liberal economic policy**, because it relies on the market and competition.

Smartvote only shows who gave **similar answers**. You do not have to vote according to the recommendation; each person has to decide for themselves. In Germany there is a similar voting aid, the **Wahl-O-Mat**. It compares the voters' positions with those of the parties. Smartvote also compares individual candidates.

gewusst: With Smartvote you can compare not only parties but also individual candidates with your own views.
The Smartspider is called that because the chart looks like a spider's web.

teile.einleitung: The Swiss parliament does not meet all year round, but several times a year for a few weeks. This period is called a session. During the session, the National Council and the Council of States debate laws and vote.
wichtigste: A session is the period in which parliament sits.
There are four ordinary sessions a year.
They are called the spring, summer, autumn and winter sessions.
An ordinary session lasts about three weeks.
At the end of each session there are the final votes.
When there is a lot of business, a special session can take place.

abschnitte.text: A **session** is the period in which parliament comes together. The sessions take place in the **Parliament Building** in Bern, which is also called the Federal Palace. Only in exceptional cases has parliament sat somewhere else. Between sessions, the members go back to their work. Many have a job besides politics.

There are four **ordinary sessions**. They are named after the seasons: the **spring, summer, autumn and winter sessions**. Each lasts about **three weeks**. Together that makes 4 times 3, so 12 weeks a year. The winter session begins at the end of November and lasts into **December**. In this session parliament also elects its new presidents.

On the last Friday of a session the **final votes** take place. Then both chambers vote once and for all on the laws they have finished debating. Only when both chambers say yes is a law passed. After that, the people can still call a **referendum**.

Sometimes there is so much business that the four sessions are not enough. Then a **special session** can take place. It comes on top of the four ordinary sessions. For urgent questions there are also **extraordinary sessions**.

gewusst: The Swiss parliament only sits for about twelve weeks a year, because it is a militia parliament.
The four sessions are named after the four seasons.

teile.einleitung: The Swiss People's Party, SVP for short, is one of the big parties in Switzerland. Since 1999 it has been the party with the most votes in elections to the National Council. It is especially committed to Switzerland's independence.
wichtigste: The SVP was founded in 1971, mainly from the Farmers, Trades and Citizens' Party (BGB).
Its colour is green, and its logo shows a bright yellow sun.
Since 1999 it has been the party with the most votes in Switzerland.
Its best result was 29.4 per cent in 2015.
It is against Switzerland joining the EU.
In 2025 Guy Parmelin and Albert Rösti sat on the Federal Council for the SVP.

abschnitte.text: The SVP has its roots in the **Farmers, Trades and Citizens' Party**, BGB for short. The Bernese farmer **Rudolf Minger** was the first BGB politician to be elected to the Federal Council, in 1929. In 1971 the BGB merged with the Democratic Parties of the cantons of Glarus and the Grisons. This is how the SVP came about. The **green logo** with a yellow sun is a reminder of its farming roots.

For a long time the SVP was a rather small party in the Federal Council. In the 1990s it grew strongly. In the elections of **1999** it won 22.5 per cent and came ahead of the SP and the FDP for the first time. Since then it has been the **party with the most votes** without a break. Its record result came in **2015** with 29.4 per cent. That is the highest share of any party since proportional representation was introduced.

The SVP is seen as **right-wing conservative**. It stands for an independent Switzerland and is against **joining the EU**. Important topics for it are immigration, neutrality and low taxes. It often brings its concerns to the people with popular initiatives. The **deportation initiative** was accepted on 28 November 2010. Other initiatives, such as the limitation initiative, were rejected. Opponents criticise its positions, while supporters value it as a clear voice.

The SVP has two members on the Federal Council. In 2025 these were **Guy Parmelin**, in office since 2016, and **Albert Rösti**, since 2023. Rösti followed Ueli Maurer, who stepped down at the end of 2022. Since 2024 the president of the SVP Switzerland has been **Marcel Dettling** from the canton of Schwyz. He followed Marco Chiesa.

gewusst: With 29.4 per cent in 2015, the SVP reached the highest share of the vote of any party since proportional representation was introduced.
The sun in the SVP logo and the green colour are reminders of its origins as a farmers' party.

teile.einleitung: The Swiss Civil Code, ZGB for short, governs many everyday matters between people. For example, it decides when you come of age, who owns a thing and who inherits after someone dies. It has applied throughout Switzerland since 1912.
wichtigste: The Civil Code was written by the lawyer Eugen Huber.
It was passed in 1907 and has applied since 1 January 1912.
Under the Civil Code you come of age at 18.
Inheritance law governs who inherits.
Property law governs ownership and possession.
Article 2 requires people to act in good faith.
Turkey adopted the Civil Code almost completely in 1926.

abschnitte.titel: One law for all of Switzerland
abschnitte.text: In the past, every canton had its own **private law**. Private law governs relations between people, for example when buying, inheriting or within the family. On behalf of the Confederation, the lawyer **Eugen Huber** wrote a draft for a shared law. Parliament passed the Civil Code in **1907**. It came into force on **1 January 1912**. Eugen Huber is therefore regarded as the father of the Civil Code.

The **law of persons** says, for example, when you **come of age**. According to Article 14, you are of age once you have reached the age of 18. Until 1996 the limit was still 20. **Family law** governs, among other things, marriage and the relationship between parents and children.

**Inheritance law** governs who receives someone's assets after they die. It also decides when a **will** is valid and what **compulsory share** close relatives receive. **Property law** decides who owns a thing or a piece of land and how you acquire ownership. This also includes the **land register**, in which all plots of land are recorded.

Article 1 allows the court something special: if there is neither a law nor customary law, it decides according to the rule it would make **as legislator**. This article is regarded as very modern. Article 2 requires everyone to act in **good faith**, that is, honestly and fairly. Obvious abuse of a right is not protected.

The Civil Code is written clearly and is easy to understand. That is why it also served other countries as a model. **Turkey** adopted it almost completely in 1926 when it modernised its law. For this, it was translated into Turkish.

gewusst: A Swiss code of law became almost completely the law of Turkey in 1926.
Until 1996 you only came of age in Switzerland at 20.

teile.einleitung: In the canton of Appenzell Innerrhoden, people vote in the open air at the Landsgemeinde. There, men may show a side arm instead of a paper identity card. A side arm is a bladed weapon that you wear at your side, for example a sword or a sabre.
wichtigste: In Appenzell Innerrhoden the side arm counts as a voting card for men.
Swords, sabres and bayonets count as side arms.
A sword of this kind has a long, narrow blade.
Many swords are passed down in the family.
Women, and men too, can show the paper voting card.

abschnitte.text: A **side arm** is not a firearm but a **bladed weapon**. You wear it in a sheath on your belt at the hip, that is, at your side. A **sword** of this kind has a long, narrow metal blade. The **sabre** and the **bayonet** also count. A bayonet is a blade that can also be fixed onto a rifle.

abschnitte.titel: The voting card at the Landsgemeinde
abschnitte.text: At the **Landsgemeinde** in Appenzell Innerrhoden, the people entitled to vote gather in a square and vote by raising their hands. There, men may show their side arm as a **voting card**. Women show the paper voting card. Men may also use this card. Many swords are passed on by a father or grandfather and are a valuable **heirloom**.

In the past, it was mainly the men who **defended** the land in war who were allowed to have a say. The weapon therefore showed that someone was a full citizen and could take part in decisions. Today the side arm is above all a **tradition**. It is a reminder of the long history of the Landsgemeinde.

gewusst: In Appenzell Innerrhoden an old family sword can serve as a card for voting.
Despite its German name, which contains the word for “gun”, the side arm is not a firearm but a blade.

teile.einleitung: The Swiss cross is a white cross on a red background. It is the best-known symbol of Switzerland and appears on the flag, on the passport and on many products. The Swiss flag has a special shape: it is square.
wichtigste: The Swiss cross is white and stands free on a red background.
On land the Swiss flag is square.
Only Switzerland and Vatican City have a square flag.
On ships the Swiss flag is rectangular.
The symbol of the Red Cross is the Swiss flag with the colours swapped.
On 1 August many people hang out the flag.

abschnitte.text: The Swiss flag is **square**, which means it is as high as it is wide. That is very rare for national flags. Only **Vatican City** also has a square flag. The white cross stands **free in the middle** and does not touch the edge. On **ships**, however, a rectangular Swiss flag flies, as is usual everywhere on the water.

On **1 August** Switzerland celebrates its national day. Many people then hang the flag on their house or balcony. That way they show they are joining in the celebrations. On this day you also often see the Swiss cross on paper lanterns, napkins and cakes.

Many products carry the Swiss cross. It shows that they come **from Switzerland**. The cross is seen as a sign of quality. That is why there are rules: not every product may simply carry the cross; it must really come largely from Switzerland.

The **Red Cross** is an aid organisation that was founded in Switzerland. It was **Henry Dunant** from Geneva who inspired its founding. For this he received the first **Nobel Peace Prize** in 1901. In honour of Switzerland, its flag with the **colours swapped** was chosen as the symbol: a red cross on a white background.

gewusst: In the whole world only two countries have a square flag: Switzerland and Vatican City.
The symbol of the Red Cross is a reversed Swiss flag.

teile.einleitung: The Federal Assembly, that is, the National Council and the Council of States together, works in sessions. These are periods of a few weeks in which parliament sits in Bern. Each session has its fixed routine and its typical business.
wichtigste: The Federal Assembly is a militia parliament and therefore sits in sessions.
In the winter session after the elections, the whole Federal Council is elected.
In the summer session the state accounts are approved.
Tuesday afternoon is set aside for parliamentary group meetings.
On Mondays the National Council only starts at 2.30 pm.
The first session outside Bern took place in Geneva in 1993.

abschnitte.text: Most members of parliament have a **job** alongside their seat. That is why the Federal Assembly is called a **militia parliament**. For this reason it does not meet all year round, but only for a few weeks in **sessions**. In between, the **committees** work. There, smaller groups of members prepare the business.

On **Monday** the National Council only begins at **2.30 pm**, so that members from all over Switzerland can travel there. On the other days it starts at 8 am. **Tuesday afternoon** is kept free: then the **parliamentary groups**, that is, the groups of the parties, hold their discussions. When there is a lot of business, there is an **evening sitting** from 7 pm to 10 pm, usually on the Monday of the second week of the session.

Some business always comes in the same session. The **state accounts** for the previous year show how much money the Confederation took in and spent. They are approved in the **summer session** in June. The **budget** for the next year only comes in winter. After the National Council elections in October, the new legislative period begins with the **winter session**. There, in December, the United Federal Assembly elects the whole **Federal Council**.

Normally parliament sits in the Federal Palace in Bern. But the **autumn session of 1993** took place in **Geneva**, the first session outside Bern. Later, further sessions followed in other parts of the country. In May and June 2020 the chambers met on the **Bernexpo** grounds because of the **COVID-19 pandemic**, because distances could not be kept in the Federal Palace.

gewusst: On Monday the National Council only starts in the afternoon, so that everyone can travel to Bern in time.
The whole Federal Council is always re-elected in December after the National Council elections.

teile.einleitung: The Sonderbund War of 1847 was the last war on Swiss soil. Liberal and Catholic-conservative cantons argued about how Switzerland should be organised. After the war, the modern federal state was created in 1848.
wichtigste: In 1845 seven Catholic-conservative cantons founded the **Sonderbund**.
Inviting the Jesuits to Lucerne made the dispute worse.
On 4 November 1847 the Diet decided to dissolve the Sonderbund by force of arms.
General **Guillaume-Henri Dufour** led the federal troops.
The battle of Gisikon on 23 November 1847 was decisive.
Valais was the last canton to surrender, on 29 November 1847.
The war lasted only a few weeks.

abschnitte.text: In the first half of the 19th century, Switzerland was a loose league of cantons, governed by the Federal Treaty of 1815. The **Liberals** wanted a strong federal state with shared laws. The **Catholic-conservative** cantons feared losing their independence and their faith. When Lucerne invited the **Jesuits** to its higher schools, the Liberals were outraged. This was followed by the Freischaren expeditions, that is, armed marches by volunteers against Lucerne.

On 11 December 1845 seven cantons joined together in Lucerne to form a protective alliance: Lucerne, Uri, Schwyz, Unterwalden, Zug, Fribourg and Valais. Obwalden and Nidwalden were counted together as Unterwalden. The majority of the **Diet**, the assembly of the cantons, saw this as a breach of the Federal Treaty. The Sonderbund cantons hoped for help from **Austria**. But this help never came, because the conservative powers had problems of their own.

On 4 November 1847 the Diet in Bern decided to dissolve the Sonderbund by force of arms. General **Guillaume-Henri Dufour** led the federal troops and tried to avoid casualties as far as possible. The Sonderbund army was under the command of **Johann Ulrich von Salis-Soglio**, a Protestant from the Grisons. On 23 November the decision came at the battle of **Gisikon** on the River Reuss. The following day Lucerne was occupied.

After Lucerne, the other Sonderbund cantons gave up too. **Valais** was the last canton to surrender, on 29 November 1847. So the war lasted just under four weeks. Because Dufour acted quickly and carefully, there were comparatively few deaths. This helped the opponents to make peace again after the war.

After the Liberals' victory, the **Federal Constitution of 1848** was created. The loose confederation of states became a federal state with a Federal Council and a Federal Assembly. But the cantons kept many rights, which is called **federalism**. The Sonderbund War is regarded as the last war in Switzerland. To this day the Dufourspitze, the highest peak in Switzerland, is a reminder of the general.

gewusst: The Dufourspitze in the Monte Rosa massif is named after General Dufour.
The commander-in-chief of the Catholic Sonderbund was himself a Protestant.
Only about half a year after the end of the war, the new Federal Constitution was accepted in 1848.

teile.einleitung: The Swiss Trade Union Federation, SGB for short, is the largest umbrella organisation of employees in Switzerland. Many individual trade unions are joined together in it. It campaigns for good wages, good working conditions and secure pensions.
wichtigste: The SGB was founded in 1880.
It represents the interests of employees.
Its largest member union is Unia.
The VPOD organises staff in the public service.
In 2024 the people and the cantons accepted the initiative for a 13th AVS pension.
The minimum wage initiative was clearly rejected in 2014.
The SGB has traditionally been close to the SP.

abschnitte.text: A **trade union** is an association of employees. Together they carry more weight when they negotiate wages and working hours with employers. The SGB is an **umbrella organisation** of such unions. It was founded in **1880**, which makes it one of the oldest umbrella organisations in Switzerland. It represents its members' concerns to politicians and employers.

The largest trade union in Switzerland is **Unia**. It was formed in 2004 mainly from the GBI, the SMUV and the VHTL, that is, from unions for construction, industry and trade. Unia organises workers in construction, industry, trades and private services. The **VPOD** represents employees of the Confederation, the cantons, the municipalities and public companies. The **SEV** union mainly organises transport staff.

abschnitte.titel: Wins and defeats at the ballot box
abschnitte.text: The SGB also launches **popular initiatives**. In May 2014 the minimum wage initiative called for a national minimum wage of 22 francs an hour. About 76 per cent of voters rejected it. On **3 March 2024**, however, the people and the cantons accepted the initiative for a **13th AVS pension**. For an initiative from the trade unions, that was unusual.

Historically, the SGB has been close to **social democracy**. Many of its leading figures sit in the federal parliament for the **SP**. Its counterpart in the social partnership is the employers' associations. The trade unions often negotiate **collective labour agreements** with them, which set out wages and working hours.

gewusst: With the 13th AVS pension, the trade unions won a vote in 2024 that many people had not expected.
Unia was formed in 2004 from several unions and is now the largest in Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: The Swiss Trade Association, SGV for short, is the umbrella organisation of Switzerland's small and medium-sized enterprises. These include, for example, bakeries, joiners' workshops, hairdressing salons and engineering offices. It was founded in 1879 and has its headquarters in Bern.
wichtigste: The SGV represents small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs).
SMEs have fewer than 250 employees.
Over 99 per cent of Swiss companies are SMEs.
The SGV was founded in 1879 and has its headquarters in Bern.
It fights for less bureaucracy and lower regulatory costs.
It is strongly committed to dual vocational training.

abschnitte.text: **SME** stands for small and medium-sized enterprises. According to the Federal Statistical Office, these are companies with fewer than **250 employees**. Larger companies are called large enterprises. Over 99 per cent of all companies in Switzerland are SMEs. The SGV is their **umbrella organisation** and represents their concerns in politics.

The Trade Association was founded in **1879**. This makes it a little older than the Swiss Trade Union Federation. Its headquarters are in **Bern**, near the Federal Palace. So it is close to what happens in politics. Every year it holds the “Trade Winter Conference” in **Klosters**. There, representatives of trade and politicians discuss economic policy.

An important concern of the SGV is **reducing regulatory costs**. Rules and forms are often a bigger burden for small firms than for large ones. After all, a small business has no department of its own to deal with them. The SGV therefore campaigns for less regulation and lower administrative costs.

A large share of apprenticeships are offered by SMEs. That is why **dual vocational training** is very important to the SGV. “Dual” means twofold: you learn at the **training company** and at the **vocational school**. The association also publishes a newspaper, the **Schweizerische Gewerbezeitung**.

gewusst: Almost all companies in Switzerland are SMEs: over 99 per cent.
The Trade Association is a year older than the Swiss Trade Union Federation.

teile.einleitung: The Swiss Employers' Association represents employers, that is, companies that hire people. It deals with questions about the labour market, education and social insurance. Its counterpart is the trade unions.
wichtigste: The association was founded in 1908 and has its headquarters in Zurich.
It is an umbrella organisation of industry and regional employers' organisations.
It deals with the labour market, education and social policy.
It represents Swiss employers in the International Labour Organization.
It relies on social partnership with the trade unions.
It usually opposes minimum wages set by law.

abschnitte.text: The Employers' Association is an **umbrella organisation**. Its members are mainly **industry associations**, regional employers' organisations and a few individual companies. Together they represent a large share of the people employed in Switzerland. The association has its headquarters in **Zurich**.

The association was founded in **1908** as the “Central Association of Swiss Employers' Organisations”. It was a reaction to the trade unions, which were growing stronger at the time. It kept this old name until 1996. Today it is called the Swiss Employers' Association.

In Switzerland, employers and trade unions often negotiate wages and working conditions themselves. This is called **social partnership**. The results are usually set out in **collective labour agreements**, GAV for short. The state only steps in to add to them. That is why the Employers' Association usually opposes **minimum wages** set by law. For example, it fought against the minimum wage initiative of 2014. The trade unions see it differently and call for minimum wages.

The **AVS** and the pension fund (**BVG**) are largely funded through contributions from wages. Employers and employees pay these together. That is why the Employers' Association has a strong say in pension reforms. **Vocational training** is also important to it, because companies offer many apprenticeships.

The **International Labour Organization** (ILO) has its headquarters in Geneva. It has a three-part structure: governments, employers and workers work together in it. Swiss employers are represented there by the Employers' Association.

gewusst: In the International Labour Organization in Geneva, states, employers and workers sit at one table.
The Employers' Association was founded because the trade unions were becoming stronger and stronger.

teile.einleitung: A swimming pool is a place where you can swim, play and cool down. In Switzerland people often say “Badi”. Many municipalities have their own Badi or an indoor pool.
wichtigste: In Switzerland the outdoor pool is often called “Badi”.
An indoor pool is under a roof and is open in winter too.
The lifeguard makes sure that nobody drowns.
You shower before swimming.
You do not run at the edge of the pool, because it is slippery.
Children who cannot swim always need someone watching them.

abschnitte.text: An **outdoor pool** is in the open air and is open mainly in summer. In Switzerland it is often called a **Badi**. An **indoor pool** is in a building. That is why you can swim there all year round, even in winter. Many swimming pools belong to the **municipality**. It provides them for the people and for school swimming lessons.

A **lifeguard** works at the swimming pool. They watch the water closely. In an emergency they rescue people and give **first aid**. What they say applies to everyone at the pool. That way swimming stays safe for everyone.

Before swimming you **shower**. That way the water in the pool stays cleaner. You do not run at the **edge of the pool**, because the floor is wet and slippery. If you run, you can fall and hurt yourself. You only jump into the water where it is allowed and deep enough.

In the **non-swimmers' pool** the water is not deep. There children can stand and play safely. **Armbands** help with practising, but they do not replace someone watching. Children who cannot swim always need an adult nearby. At school or on a course, many children learn to **swim** and how to stay safe in the water.

gewusst: The word “Badi” is typically Swiss; in Germany people tend to say “Freibad”.
Armbands help with practising, but they never replace an adult who is keeping watch.

teile.einleitung: A semi-presidential system of government is a mixed form. There is a strong president elected by the people and also a prime minister who needs the confidence of parliament. The best-known example is France.
wichtigste: In a semi-presidential system the president and the prime minister share power.
The president is elected by the people and is independent of parliament.
The prime minister needs a majority in parliament.
France is the classic example, shaped by Charles de Gaulle.
Today the French president is elected for five years.
When the president and the prime minister come from opposing camps, this is called cohabitation.

abschnitte.text: There are different ways of governing a country. In a **presidential system** such as in the USA, the president leads the government alone. In a **parliamentary system**, parliament elects the government. The **semi-presidential system** lies in between. “Semi” means half. Power is divided between the **president** and the **prime minister**. The president is independent of parliament, whereas the prime minister needs its confidence.

The constitution of the **Fifth Republic** of 1958 was shaped by **Charles de Gaulle**. He wanted a strong president and became the first president himself in 1959. The president is elected directly by the **people**. If nobody wins an absolute majority in the first round, there is a **run-off** between the two candidates with the most votes. From 1873 the term of office lasted seven years, the “septennat”. A referendum in 2000 shortened it to **five years** from the 2002 election onwards.

In France the president **appoints** the prime minister. But the prime minister needs a majority in the **National Assembly**, otherwise he or she can be brought down. In turn, the president may **dissolve** the National Assembly and call new elections, at most once a year. Emmanuel Macron did this, for example, in June 2024.

Sometimes a different political camp from the president's wins the parliamentary election. Then the president has to appoint a prime minister from the opposing camp. This is called **cohabitation**, meaning “living together”. It happened, for example, from 1986 to 1988, when President **François Mitterrand** had to govern with Prime Minister **Jacques Chirac**.

The political scientists **Shugart and Carey** distinguish two sub-types. In the **premier-presidential** system, only parliament can dismiss the government. In the **president-parliamentary** system, the president can do so as well. Switzerland has a completely different system: here the seven-member Federal Council governs together, and there is no president with a lot of power.

gewusst: In France it can happen that the president and the prime minister are political opponents and still have to govern together.
The French president used to be elected for seven years.

teile.einleitung: The Swiss Psalm is the national anthem of Switzerland. A national anthem is a solemn song that stands for a whole country. People sing the Swiss Psalm on 1 August and hear it before international matches.
wichtigste: The tune was written by the monk Alberich Zwyssig in 1841.
The German text was written by Leonhard Widmer from Zurich.
In 1961 the Swiss Psalm became the anthem on a provisional basis.
Since 1981 it has officially been the national anthem.
In French it begins with “Sur nos monts, quand le soleil”.
In the past “Rufst du, mein Vaterland” was the anthem.

abschnitte.text: **Alberich Zwyssig** was a **monk** at Wettingen Abbey. He was also a musician and composer. **Leonhard Widmer** from Zurich wrote a text and gave it to Zwyssig, who set it to music in **1841**. This is how the Swiss Psalm came about. A **psalm** is a solemn, religious song.

Before the Swiss Psalm became the anthem, people sang “**Rufst du, mein Vaterland**” for a long time. But this song had the same tune as the English anthem. When both countries met at an event, this often led to mix-ups. That is why a separate anthem was looked for.

abschnitte.titel: The road to the official anthem
abschnitte.text: In **1961** the Federal Council first declared the Swiss Psalm the anthem only **provisionally**. Provisionally means for the time being, on trial. Only in **1981** did it finally become the official national anthem. So twenty years passed in between.

The Swiss Psalm exists in all the **national languages**. In French it begins with “Sur nos monts, quand le soleil”. Do not mix it up: “Allons enfants de la patrie” is the beginning of the French anthem, the Marseillaise. On **1 August** the Swiss Psalm is sung at many celebrations, and it is also played before international matches.

gewusst: The former Swiss anthem had the same tune as the English anthem.
For twenty years the Swiss Psalm was only an anthem on trial.

teile.einleitung: Public service means basic provision: important services should be available to all people in all regions of Switzerland in good quality and at fair prices. These include, for example, the post, public transport, radio and television, electricity and water.
wichtigste: Public service means basic provision for all regions.
The federal post has existed since 1849.
In 1998 the PTT was split into Swiss Post and Swisscom.
Swiss Post has a remaining monopoly on letters up to 50 grams.
The SBB came about after a popular vote in 1898.
The SBB belongs entirely to the Confederation.
In 1982 the SBB introduced the regular-interval timetable.

abschnitte.text: **Public service** is meant to make sure that it is not only towns that are well served. A mountain village should also receive post, be reachable by bus and have electricity. That is why people speak of **basic provision**. Many of these services are provided by companies that belong wholly or partly to the Confederation, the cantons or the municipalities.

Shortly after the federal state was founded, the Confederation took over the postal service from the cantons on **1 January 1849**. Later the **PTT** came about, which stood for post, telephone, telegraph. In **1998** it was split up: the postal services went to **Swiss Post**, telecommunications to **Swisscom**. In 2025 Swiss Post has a **remaining monopoly** on domestic letters up to 50 grams. With this it funds part of the basic provision.

The **Postal Ordinance** sets out how close a post office must be. 90 per cent of the permanent resident population must be able to reach a post office or a **postal agency** within **20 minutes**, on foot or by public transport. A postal agency is, for example, a counter in a village shop.

In the past, the big railways belonged to private companies. On **20 February 1898** the people agreed that the Confederation should buy them. From **1902** the **SBB** began operating. Since 1999 it has been a public limited company whose shares all belong to the Confederation. In **1982** the SBB introduced the **regular-interval timetable**. Since then trains leave, for example, at the same minute every hour. This makes connections easier and train travel easy to plan.

gewusst: Thanks to the regular-interval timetable of 1982, many trains in Switzerland leave at the same minute every hour.
The people decided at the ballot box in 1898 that Switzerland should have a state railway.

teile.einleitung: A social bot is a computer program that runs an account on social networks and pretends to be a human. Such bots can spread opinions and make topics seem bigger than they are. That is why it is important for democracy to recognise them.
wichtigste: Social bots are programs that post, share and like automatically.
Many controlled accounts can push a hashtag into the trends artificially.
Faking a citizens' movement is called **astroturfing**.
A **sock puppet** is a disguised account with a false identity.
The Internet Research Agency from St Petersburg became known as a “troll factory”.
Tools such as Botometer only give probabilities, not certainty.

abschnitte.text: A **social bot** is a program that operates an account on a platform such as X, Facebook or Instagram on its own. It can write posts, share, comment and like. Some bots are harmless and report the weather or the news, for example. It becomes a problem when a bot pretends to be a real person. Then readers can no longer tell who is really behind an opinion.

Many coordinated accounts can share a topic in huge numbers in a short time. This way a hashtag ends up in the **trends**, even though hardly any real people are interested in it. A topic then seems more important or more controversial than it is among the population. If a citizens' movement is only faked in this way, it is called **astroturfing**. The name comes from the artificial grass brand AstroTurf and is a play on real “grassroots movements”.

A **sock puppet** is a second account that a person uses to fake a false identity. This creates seemingly independent voices that support the person's own opinion. If many such accounts are controlled automatically, they are called bots. A **troll factory** runs a very large number of fake accounts at once. The **Internet Research Agency** from St Petersburg became well known; according to the report by special counsel Robert Mueller, it tried to influence the mood before the 2016 US election.

A typical sign is an account that publishes a very large number of posts around the clock. People sleep and post irregularly; bots need no break. Other signs are new accounts, names with lots of numbers and texts that are always the same. Indiana University has developed the tool **Botometer**, which analyses activity, network and language. But it only calculates a probability and can be wrong.

As early as 1950, the mathematician **Alan Turing** presented the imitation game, now called the Turing test. In it, a person has to find out in a text conversation whether they are talking to a human or a machine. Modern chatbots now write very naturally. That is why it is becoming harder and harder to tell bots from humans. This makes it all the more important to check sources and not to trust every account blindly.

gewusst: The word “bot” is short for “robot”.
The term astroturfing comes from a brand of artificial grass.
The Turing test was thought up as early as 1950, long before there was social media.

teile.einleitung: The Swiss Broadcasting Corporation, SRG for short, makes radio, television and online content in all four national languages. It has a mission known as “public service”. It is funded mainly by the radio and television fee.
wichtigste: The SRG broadcasts in German, French, Italian and Romansh.
Its companies are called SRF, RTS, RSI and RTR.
Swissinfo informs the world about Switzerland in ten languages.
Play Suisse shows Swiss films and series with subtitles.
Since 2021 a private household has paid a fee of 335 francs a year.
Since November 2024 Susanne Wille has been Director General.

abschnitte.text: The SRG is made up of several companies. **SRF** broadcasts in German, **RTS** in French and **RSI** in Italian. **RTR** stands for Radiotelevisiun Svizra Rumantscha and broadcasts in Romansh. There is also **Swissinfo**, which informs Swiss people living abroad and an international audience in ten languages.

Article 93 of the **Federal Constitution** describes what radio and television should achieve. They should contribute to **education**, cultural development, the **free forming of opinions** and entertainment. In doing so, they must take into account the special features of the country and the needs of the cantons. This mission is called **public service**.

**Play Suisse** is a streaming platform of the SRG. It has Swiss films, series and documentaries from all language regions. They are subtitled in several national languages. So you can, for example, follow a series from Ticino with German subtitles. This is meant to encourage exchange between the language regions.

Almost all households pay the **radio and television fee**. Since 2021 it has been 335 francs a year for a private household. The Federal Council has decided to lower it step by step to 312 francs from 2027 and 300 francs from 2029. The SRG receives most of it, because it has to offer a comparable service in all four national languages. The smaller language regions receive more money than they bring in themselves. Local private broadcasters also receive a share.

The SRG is run by a **Director General**. Since November 2024 this has been **Susanne Wille**. She followed Gilles Marchand. Before that, from 2020, she was head of culture at SRF and a member of its executive board.

gewusst: The small Romansh-speaking region has its own radio and television with RTR.
Because all language regions are meant to be served equally well, money flows from German-speaking Switzerland to the smaller regions.

tswkxw2.t: Distribution of seats in the National Council

teile.einleitung: The National Council has 200 seats. They are shared out among the cantons according to the number of people living in each canton. Large cantons therefore have many seats, small ones only a few.
wichtigste: Since 1962 the National Council has been fixed at 200 seats.
The seats are shared out using the Hare/Niemeyer method.
The basis is the permanent resident population; foreign residents also count.
Every canton has at least one seat.
At the 2023 election six cantons had only one seat.
For the 2023 election one seat went from Basel-Stadt to Zurich.

abschnitte.text: In the past, the National Council grew with the population, because there was one seat for a fixed number of inhabitants. Since a **constitutional amendment in 1962**, exactly **200 seats** are always shared out. The seats are divided among the cantons according to the **permanent resident population**. This also includes foreign residents, even though they are not allowed to vote at federal level. Every canton receives at least one seat.

Sharing out the seats needs a rule of calculation. Switzerland uses the **Hare/Niemeyer** method. First, it is worked out exactly how many seats a canton would be entitled to. Usually this does not give a whole number. Each canton first gets its whole seats. The remaining seats go to the cantons with the largest **remainders** after the decimal point.

At the 2023 election **Zurich** had the most seats, namely 36. It was followed by **Bern** with 24, **Vaud** with 19 and **Aargau** with 16. **St Gallen** and **Geneva** had 12 seats each. Six cantons had only one seat: Uri, Obwalden, Nidwalden, Glarus, Appenzell Ausserrhoden and Appenzell Innerrhoden. There, one seat cannot be divided by percentages. That is why the vote uses the **majority system**: the person with the most votes wins.

If the population of a canton grows faster than elsewhere, it can gain seats. Other cantons then lose seats. For the 2023 election, one seat went from **Basel-Stadt** to **Zurich**. Since then Basel-Stadt has had four seats instead of five. **Bern** still had 33 seats in 1963, but only 24 in 2023. That is 9 seats fewer, because other cantons have grown faster.

gewusst: The canton of Bern has lost nine National Council seats since 1963, even though its population has grown.
People without a Swiss passport also count when the seats are shared out among the cantons.
